title: T1.3: Plans Data Lifecycle
description: Test your knowledge of data lifecycle planning in InterSystems IRIS, including storage/retrieval strategies, CRUD operations, and performance prediction

questions.question: A healthcare application needs to display a dashboard showing patient admission trends across multiple hospitals, grouped by month, region, and diagnosis. Which data access strategy is MOST appropriate for this scenario?

options.text: Object access using %OpenId() to iterate through patient records
SQL SELECT with GROUP BY clauses for aggregations
MDX queries against a Business Intelligence cube
Dynamic SQL with embedded cursors

questions.explanation: MDX (Multidimensional Expressions) is specifically designed for analytical queries involving dimensions, hierarchies, and aggregations across groups. This dashboard requires multidimensional analysis (time, geography, diagnosis) with automatic aggregation - exactly what MDX cubes provide. While SQL can perform aggregations, MDX is optimized for OLAP/BI scenarios with complex pivot table displays. Object access would be extremely inefficient for aggregating across many records. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=D2GMDX_intro_mdx

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describe when to use SQL access versus object access in InterSystems IRIS?

options.text: Object access is preferred for single-record transactional operations with business logic
SQL is optimal for set-based operations across multiple records
Object access automatically handles swizzling for lazy loading of related objects
SQL should always be used instead of object access for better performance

questions.explanation: Object access is ideal for single-record operations with business logic encapsulation and provides automatic swizzling for related objects. SQL excels at set-based operations for querying, filtering, and aggregating multiple records. The choice depends on use case - object access for transactional operations, SQL for reporting and batch operations. The statement that SQL should always be used is incorrect; object access provides better performance for single-record CRUD operations. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ

questions.question:
An application performs frequent updates to individual customer records based on user interactions. Which access pattern offers the BEST combination of performance and maintainability?

```objectscript
Set customer = ##class(MyApp.Customer).%OpenId(customerId)
If $IsObject(customer) {
    Set customer.LastContactDate = $HOROLOG
    Set customer.ContactCount = customer.ContactCount + 1
    Set sc = customer.%Save()
}
```

options.text: MDX queries for analytical performance
Object access as shown above for transactional operations
Dynamic SQL UPDATE statements for better concurrency
Embedded SQL with cursors for row-by-row processing

questions.explanation: Object access is optimal for single-record transactional operations. It provides strong typing, automatic property validation, business logic encapsulation through methods, and swizzling for related objects. The %Save() method handles all persistence atomically with transaction support. SQL would add unnecessary overhead for single-record updates, and MDX is for analytical queries, not transactional updates. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ

questions.question: A reporting system needs to generate monthly sales summaries for 50,000+ transactions. The report aggregates data by product category, region, and sales representative. What is the MOST efficient data access approach?

options.text: Use %OpenId() to iterate through all transaction objects and calculate totals in ObjectScript
Execute a SQL SELECT with GROUP BY clauses for aggregations
Load all objects into a local array and use $ORDER to calculate totals
Use MDX only if a Business Intelligence cube has been pre-defined

questions.explanation: SQL is specifically optimized for set-based operations like aggregations across large datasets. The query optimizer will use appropriate indexes and generate efficient execution plans for GROUP BY operations. Object iteration would be extremely inefficient, requiring 50,000+ object loads and manual aggregation logic. While MDX could be used if a cube exists, SQL provides excellent performance for standard aggregations without requiring pre-built cubes. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GSQL

questions.question:
What is the correct sequence of operations to create and persist a new object in InterSystems IRIS?

```objectscript
// Option A
Set obj = ##class(MyApp.Order).%New()
Set obj.OrderDate = $HOROLOG
Set obj.CustomerId = 12345
Set sc = obj.%Save()
If $$$ISERR(sc) Do $System.Status.DisplayError(sc)
```

options.text: The code above is correct - %New(), set properties, %Save(), check status
%New() should be called with parameters: %New(OrderDate, CustomerId)
%Save() should be called before setting properties
%Insert() should be used instead of %Save() for new objects

questions.explanation: The correct create sequence is: (1) instantiate with %New(), (2) set property values, (3) call %Save() to persist, (4) check the returned %Status value. %Save() automatically determines if this is a new object (insert) or existing object (update). While constructors can accept parameters if defined, the shown pattern is the standard approach. %Insert() is not a standard persistence API method. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ

questions.question: Which statements about the %Save() method in InterSystems IRIS are TRUE?

options.text: %Save() returns a %Status value indicating success or failure
%Save() automatically saves embedded objects, collections, and streams
%Save() executes atomically - it either saves everything or rolls back completely
%Save() always creates a new object ID using $Increment
%Save() calls %OnBeforeSave() and %OnAfterSave() callback methods
Failed %Save() operations leave partial data in the database

questions.explanation: %Save() returns a %Status value for error checking, automatically saves all related objects (embedded, collections, streams), executes atomically with automatic rollback on failure, and calls callback hooks for business logic. However, object IDs are only auto-generated if not specified by an IDKEY index, and failed saves do NOT leave partial data - the atomic nature ensures complete rollback. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ

questions.question:
An application needs to read a Customer object and its related Company information. Which code snippet demonstrates proper object opening with swizzling?

```objectscript
// Option 1
Set customer = ##class(MyApp.Customer).%OpenId(123, , .sc)
If $$$ISERR(sc) Quit
Set companyName = customer.Company.Name
```

options.text: The code is correct - swizzling automatically loads the Company object when accessed
The Company object must be explicitly opened: Set company = ##class(MyApp.Company).%OpenId(customer.CompanyId)
Swizzling only works if concurrency level is set to 4
The Company relationship must be defined as LAZY = 0 for swizzling to work

questions.explanation: The code correctly demonstrates swizzling. When customer.Company.Name is accessed, IRIS automatically opens (swizzles) the related Company object if not already in memory. This lazy loading happens transparently when traversing object relationships via dot syntax. No explicit %OpenId() call is needed for related objects. Swizzling works at all concurrency levels and doesn't require specific LAZY settings. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ

questions.question: What is the purpose of the concurrency parameter in %OpenId(id, concurrency, .sc) and what does a value of 0 indicate?

options.text: Concurrency 0 means no locking - maximum performance but no atomic write guarantees
Concurrency 0 means exclusive locks are held until transaction commit
Concurrency 0 is invalid and will cause an error
Concurrency 0 is the default and provides maximum data integrity

questions.explanation: Concurrency 0 means no locking is performed, providing maximum performance for read-only or single-user scenarios. However, it offers no atomic write guarantees since no locks prevent concurrent modifications. Concurrency 1 (atomic read) is the default for most operations. Concurrency levels range from 0 (no locking) to 4 (exclusive/retained locks), with higher values providing stronger isolation at the cost of performance and concurrency. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ

questions.question: A production application will have 100+ concurrent users performing frequent updates to order records. Which concurrency considerations are MOST important?

options.text: Use concurrency level 4 (exclusive/retained) for all operations to ensure data integrity
Keep transactions short with narrow scope to minimize lock duration
Higher concurrency levels provide stronger isolation but increase lock contention
Swizzling can trigger cascading lock acquisitions on related objects
Concurrency level 0 should be used for maximum performance with many users

questions.explanation: For high-concurrency applications, short transactions minimize lock contention. Higher concurrency levels (2-4) provide stronger isolation but increase contention - use the minimum level needed. Swizzling does trigger locks based on default concurrency settings. However, concurrency 4 for all operations would create excessive contention, and concurrency 0 would cause data corruption with concurrent writers. Balance is key. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ

questions.question:
You execute a SQL query in the SQL Shell and observe these performance metrics:

```
Prepare Time: 0.05s
Execute Time: 12.3s
Global References: 2,450,000
Disk I/O: 125,000
```

The query scans a table with 500,000 rows. What is the MOST likely performance issue?

options.text: High prepare time indicates query compilation issues
High global references and disk I/O suggest a full table scan without index usage
The execute time is normal for this data volume
Disk I/O is too low, indicating insufficient cache utilization

questions.explanation: The very high global references (2.45 million) and disk I/O (125,000) relative to execute time strongly suggest a full table scan. For 500,000 rows, an indexed query should require far fewer global references. Prepare time is low (good), but execute time is excessive. Using EXPLAIN/SHOW PLAN would confirm missing indexes. This pattern indicates the need for index creation on frequently queried columns. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GSQL

questions.question:
An application performs well with 1,000 customer records but slows significantly at 100,000 records. This query is used frequently:

```sql
SELECT * FROM MyApp.Customer 
WHERE LastName = 'Smith' AND State = 'CA'
```

What is the BEST approach to predict and resolve performance degradation?

options.text: Switch from SQL to object access for better performance
Use EXPLAIN to analyze the query plan and create appropriate indexes
Increase the global buffer pool size to cache more data
Reduce data volume by archiving old customer records

questions.explanation: The performance degradation with increasing data volume strongly suggests missing indexes. Use EXPLAIN/SHOW PLAN to analyze the query execution plan and identify table scan operations. Creating indexes on LastName and/or State (or a composite index on both) would dramatically improve performance. Object access would be slower for filtered queries. While buffer pool size helps, it doesn't address the root cause. Data archival doesn't solve the indexing issue. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GSQL

questions.question: Which factors should be considered when predicting application performance for a multi-user transactional system?

options.text: Data volume impacts query performance through index selection and table scan costs
Concurrent user counts affect lock contention and transaction throughput
Query execution plans remain constant regardless of data volume
Performance metrics (prepare/execute time, globals, disk I/O) enable capacity planning
Long-running transactions with broad scope reduce lock contention
The SQL query optimizer generates plans based on table statistics

questions.explanation: Performance prediction requires analyzing data volume (affecting index usage), concurrent users (affecting lock contention), and monitoring performance metrics for capacity planning. The query optimizer uses table statistics to generate plans. However, query plans DO change with data volume - small tables may use table scans while large tables require indexes. Long-running transactions INCREASE contention, not reduce it; short transactions with narrow scope minimize contention. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GSQLOPT
